findings.evidence: "The benefits team tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year."
findings.fix: Add two or three sentences describing the stipend's purpose, amount, and what it covers, or rename the section to something like "Budget Administration."
findings.violation: The section is titled "Program Overview" but never describes what the stipend program actually is, what it covers, or how much it pays; it only states an internal budget tracking schedule.

findings.evidence: "Similarly, the people operations office updates the equipment catalog each quarter."
findings.fix: Remove "Similarly" or replace it with a neutral transition such as "Separately," unless an actual parallel is intended and should be spelled out.
findings.location: Program Overview section, second paragraph, opening word
findings.violation: "Similarly" implies this sentence mirrors the one before it, but budget tracking at the start of the fiscal year and catalog updates every quarter are unrelated in both timing and subject, so the connector misstates the relationship between the two ideas.

findings.evidence: "In addition, eligibility for the workspace stipend depends on several details the reviewer checks one at a time."
findings.fix: Use one consistent name throughout the document, or add a sentence stating explicitly that "the workspace stipend" and "the home-office equipment stipend" refer to the same benefit.
findings.location: Eligibility section, third paragraph, first sentence
findings.violation: The document never states whether "the workspace stipend" is the same benefit as the "home-office equipment stipend" named in the title and the two preceding paragraphs, so a reader cannot tell if this paragraph adds conditions to the same benefit or introduces a different one.

findings.evidence: nine consecutive short sentences beginning "The workspace must sit inside the employee's primary residence...", "A workspace located in a shared coworking space...", "A workspace used only occasionally for calls..."
findings.fix: Reformat the paragraph as a bulleted list, one eligibility criterion per bullet.
findings.violation: Nine separate eligibility conditions are presented as run-on prose in a single paragraph rather than as a list, which forces the reader to parse each sentence boundary by hand and makes it easy to miss a condition.

findings.evidence: "Employees must submit the receipt, the manager's approval form, and the original purchase order before the review begins" versus "A photo of the receipt is enough for most requests."
findings.fix: State one consistent documentation requirement, or explain explicitly which cases need the original purchase order and which only need a photo of the receipt.
findings.location: How to Apply section, first paragraph, compared with Required Documentation section, first paragraph
findings.violation: One section requires the original purchase order as a mandatory submission before review begins, while another section says a photo of the receipt is enough for most requests, and the two statements are never reconciled, so the actual documentation requirement is unclear.

findings.evidence: "Additionally, employees shall retain receipts for one year after the purchase date."
findings.fix: Replace "shall" with "must" to match the modal verb used everywhere else in the document.
findings.violation: Every other obligation in the document uses "must" (for example "Employees must submit the receipt"), so the sudden switch to "shall" here is a register inconsistency that may read as a separate, stricter kind of obligation.

findings.evidence: "The finance office conducts an evaluation of every submitted receipt before it approves the amount."
findings.fix: Change the sentence to "The finance office evaluates every submitted receipt before it approves the amount."
findings.violation: The nominalized phrase "conducts an evaluation of" adds words without adding meaning compared to the plain verb "evaluates," making the sentence harder to read than it needs to be.

findings.evidence: "Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category."
findings.fix: Split the sentence into three or four shorter sentences, one idea per sentence.
findings.location: Restrictions and Exceptions section, second paragraph
findings.violation: This single sentence is roughly ninety words and bundles five separate ideas, the one-device rule, the second-device exception, the fieldwork justification, the standard-desk assumption, and the tracking method, with no punctuation break, making it very difficult to parse in one reading.

findings.evidence: "You record the stipend item on the request form." and "Also, you submit the request in the portal."
findings.fix: Replace "You" with "Employees" or "The employee" to match the third-person voice used throughout the rest of the document.
findings.violation: The rest of the document refers to the reader in the third person, for example "Employees must submit..." and "the employee reviews...," so the switch to second person "You" here is inconsistent and may leave the reader unsure whether "you" still means the employee.

findings.evidence: "You record the stipend item on the request form" and "Employees keep proof of purchase for every stipend item."
findings.fix: Define "stipend item" on first use, or replace it with an already defined term such as "equipment."
findings.location: Terminology Notes section and Required Documentation section
findings.violation: "Stipend item" is used as an established term but is never defined anywhere in the document, and its relationship to "the stipend," "the equipment," or "the workspace" is never explained.

findings.evidence: "Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt."
findings.fix: Either list the complete set of steps in this section or remove it and consolidate the process into "How to Apply."
findings.violation: This section implies it lists the steps to complete a request but names only two of the steps described earlier under "How to Apply," which also requires the manager's approval form, the purchase order, and reviewing a confirmation summary, so a reader relying on this section alone would submit an incomplete request.

findings.evidence: "The finance liaison reviews the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year. Staff can request a printed copy from the benefits team at any time."
findings.fix: Remove this section or replace it with content describing genuine special cases, such as partial-year eligibility or exceptions to the standard process.
findings.violation: This section is nearly a word-for-word repeat of the Program Overview section's first paragraph, with only "benefits team tracks" changed to "finance liaison reviews," and it does not describe any actual exceptional or special case, so the heading is misleading and the content is redundant.

findings.evidence: "The people operations office tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year. Every entry carries a date stamp so the record stays easy to audit."
findings.fix: Replace this section with guidance on who to contact for questions and how policy updates are announced, and remove the duplicated budget-tracking sentence.
findings.violation: This section repeats language from the Program Overview section almost verbatim instead of covering what its heading promises, either who to contact with questions or how policy updates are communicated, so the reader gets no answer to either question.

findings.evidence: "The escalation of repeat requests happens automatically within the same quarter."
findings.fix: Rewrite to name the actor and explain the term, for example "If an employee submits more than one stipend request in a quarter, the benefits team automatically escalates the later requests to a senior reviewer."
findings.violation: The document never explains what a "repeat request" is, why it would be escalated, or who receives the escalation, and the passive, nominalized phrasing never names who or what performs the escalation.
